summary: Describes an architecture for IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4. It combines a fast powered backbone with low-power wireless subnetworks that hop channels on a schedule, to give low latency, low jitter, and high reliability.

plainLanguage.summary: 6TiSCH carries IPv6 over wireless networks where devices transmit in scheduled time slots and change radio channels. This architecture explains how those networks connect devices, route packets, and reserve resources for predictable traffic.

questions: how does a device join a 6tisch network
subtitle: An architecture for IPv6 networks of synchronized, channel-hopping wireless devices.

tldr.problem: Low-power wireless applications can need predictable packet delivery, but devices have limited energy and share radio channels.
tldr.mechanism: 6TiSCH combines IPv6, 6LoWPAN, RPL, and the IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH schedule, with 6top exposing scheduled radio cells as IP links.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC describes the architecture for joining, routing, scheduling, and forwarding, including reserved Tracks for selected traffic.

today: RFC 9030 is an Informational architecture document published in May 2021. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes how the related 6TiSCH specifications fit together.

sections.title: Goals of the 6TiSCH Architecture
sections.content:
6TiSCH supports IPv6 connectivity for constrained wireless devices using the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) mode of IEEE 802.15.4. The RFC targets applications that need reliable packet delivery within bounded latency, including industrial and building automation.

A 6TiSCH network can combine a synchronized low-power wireless network with a faster backbone. It uses 6LoWPAN to adapt IPv6 to constrained links and the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) for distributed routing. Routes and schedules may also be computed centrally.
sections.plainLanguage: 6TiSCH connects low-power wireless devices using IPv6 and scheduled radio transmissions. The architecture can link those wireless networks through a backbone and supports both distributed and centralized control.

sections.title: The Subnet and Protocol Layers
sections.content:
In the basic configuration, one Low-Power and Lossy Network (LLN) forms an IPv6 subnet over a synchronized TSCH mesh. A 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) acts as the RPL root and as the gateway to the outside network. Because the mesh is not a broadcast link, 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery extends IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for address registration.

An extended configuration connects multiple LLNs through a wired or wireless backbone. Backbone Routers (6BBRs) proxy Neighbor Discovery for wireless nodes and synchronize across the backbone. The 6top sublayer sits between IP and the TSCH MAC and presents scheduled cells as links for IP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A small wireless mesh can form one IPv6 subnet, with a border router connecting it outward. A backbone can join multiple meshes, while special routers handle address discovery across the joined network.

sections.title: Timeslots, Cells, and Scheduling
sections.content:
TSCH divides time into timeslots and allocates communication cells by time and channel. A slotframe is a repeating collection of timeslots, and a node can use multiple slotframes for activities with different priorities. The RFC says timeslots of 10 to 15 milliseconds are typical in IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH.

6top hides the schedule details from IP and maps a link to bundles of cells for sending and receiving. Hard cells are controlled by an external scheduler and cannot be moved by 6top; soft cells can be added, removed, or moved through 6top and a Scheduling Function. The architecture describes static, neighbor-to-neighbor, centralized, and hop-by-hop scheduling; static scheduling is the only mode expected in all implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device follows a repeating timetable that assigns radio turns and channels. 6top presents those turns as links and can manage flexible cells with a neighboring device or an outside scheduler.

sections.title: Joining and Managing the Network
sections.content:
A new device, called a pledge, discovers a network through Enhanced Beacons and contacts a Join Registrar/Coordinator (JRC) through a Join Proxy (JP) that already belongs to the network. The join protocol authenticates and authorizes the device and provides network parameters over a secure channel. In the minimal pre-shared-key mode described through CoJP, joining can take one round trip with the JRC.

After joining, a device obtains a network prefix and registers its IPv6 addresses using 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery. The architecture describes several ways to manage schedules, from a static schedule to peer negotiation and central computation. RPL provides distributed routing, and the RFC recommends placing the RPL root with the 6LBR so they share information about devices.
sections.plainLanguage: A new device asks an existing neighbor to relay its join request to the network registrar. After authentication and configuration, it receives network addressing and can register its IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Tracks and Forwarding
sections.content:
A Track is a directed path through an LLN with scheduled cells and buffers reserved along the route. A Serial Track is a chain of receive and transmit cell bundles. A Complex Track is a directed acyclic graph that can provide multiple branches, including packet replication and elimination at the destination.

The architecture supports ordinary IPv6 forwarding using routing-table entries, Track Forwarding that switches frames from one timeslot to another at Layer 2, and 6LoWPAN Fragment Forwarding, where later fragments follow state established by the first fragment. Tracks can reserve resources for a path and may extend into a larger DetNet network.
sections.plainLanguage: A Track reserves cells and buffers along a path for selected traffic. It can be a simple chain or a branched route that sends copies along different paths and removes duplicates at the destination.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tracks depend on a reachable controller with a Path Computation Element. If the controller connection fails, existing Tracks may continue until their lifetime ends, but operators cannot install new ones or update existing ones. Communication with the controller and join registrar must be secured and protected against denial of service.

The TSCH hopping sequence is known, so a rogue can selectively jam a cell after identifying a flow. The RFC also describes risks to time synchronization: replaying a beacon with an old Absolute Slot Number may lead a joining device to reuse a security nonce. Link-layer security is expected after the initial join exchange, and the network may need periodic rekeying.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller outage can prevent new Tracks from being installed, and a rogue can target one flow by jamming its scheduled cell. Secure joining, trustworthy time, and key changes help protect the network.
